old: Its name is built from a Greek negation glued to the word for the red stuff running through you.
Strip away the 'not' and you're left with the Greek root for blood itself.
It shares its -emia ending with other blood-condition words, all descended from Greek haîma.
clues: This common health condition has a name that has barely changed since ancient Greek, where it already described a lack of something vital to the body.
It means having too few healthy red blood cells or too little hemoglobin, a real medical shortfall rather than ordinary tiredness. Its Greek roots literally mean 'without blood.'
Iron deficiency and sickle cell are well-known types, and its adjective form describes anything feeble, like sluggish sales or a lackluster performance.
